q: Gascony gained an appellation in 2005 for a spirit that reaches the bottle clear, having never touched wood. Name it.
exp: It rests in glass or stainless steel for at least three months and is bottled at forty percent or more, which puts a purely aromatic distillate on the table. Served very cold it does the work of a good eau-de-vie or a white rum, and it turns up in cocktails for the same reason.

q: Cognac's official ageing count begins not on the day the spirit leaves the still but on a fixed date afterwards. Which date?
exp: The compte runs from the first of April following the harvest, so an eau-de-vie distilled in February sits at compte 00 until then, becomes compte 0 on that date and reaches compte 1 a year later. Distillation itself has to be finished by the thirty-first of March, which is what fixes the date.

q: Pears are not a rounding-off in one Calvados appellation but a legal requirement, at a minimum of thirty percent. Name that appellation.
exp: The bocage around Domfront is pear country, and perry pear trees take far longer to come into bearing than apples do. The appellation also insists on a single distillation in a column still, the opposite of the double pot distillation required in the Pays d'Auge.

q: Clay and flint left by decomposed limestone give one compact Cognac cru a violet-scented spirit that comes round faster than the chalk crus do. Name that cru.
exp: It is the smallest of the six crus and sits just north of the town of Cognac itself. Grande and Petite Champagne are chalkier and much slower, while Fins Bois, Bons Bois and Bois Ordinaires ring the region and give quicker-maturing spirit still.

q: Jamaican pot still rum is bought and sold on a figure given in grams per hectolitre of pure alcohol, and the heaviest marks smell of overripe banana and glue. What is being counted?
exp: Counts run from around 100 up to a legal ceiling of 1600 grams per hectolitre in the heaviest continental flavoured marks, which are blended in tiny proportions rather than drunk neat. Long, deliberately wild fermentations are what build them.

q: The acidic liquid left in the still after a Jamaican distillation is not discarded but returned to the next fermentation to build pungency. What is that liquid called?
exp: It works like a sourdough starter, held in pits and topped up rather than made fresh each time. Together with muck, a rotting mass of cane trash and acid, it drives the ester counts that define the heavy Jamaican marks.

q: Wooden pot and Coffey stills, some of them well over a century old, still work on one river in Guyana, and the rums made on them carry that river's name. Name it.
exp: The wooden stills survived because their staves are credited with a character no metal still reproduces, so they were moved rather than scrapped as distilleries closed. The rums are dark, heavy and smoky, and were the backbone of the Royal Navy blend.

q: Brazilian law sets a minimum bottling strength for cachaca lower than the forty percent the United States demands of rum. What is it?
exp: Cachaca runs from thirty-eight to forty-eight percent and may not be distilled above fifty-four, while rum has to reach forty percent in the United States and 37.5 in the European Union. Up to six grams of sugar per litre is permitted before the drink has to be relabelled as adocada, sweetened.

q: Ships' pursers proved the strength of the rum ration by wetting gunpowder with it and setting light to the result. Which alcoholic strength does that test correspond to?
exp: Gunpowder will still flash when wetted with spirit at about fifty-seven percent and will not below it, which is where navy strength and the old 100 degrees British proof both come from. It is why a navy strength gin is bottled at 57 rather than at a round number.

q: Every bottle of Tequila carries the letters NOM followed by a four-figure number. What does that number identify?
opts: The number of times the spirit was distilled
The registered distillery that made the spirit
The field the agave was cut from
The year the agave was harvested
exp: NOM stands for Norma Oficial Mexicana, and the four figures are the distillery's registration number with the regulator. One NOM can cover many brands, since a single distillery may produce for dozens of labels, so two bottles with different names and the same NOM came off the same equipment. It is the quickest way for a buyer to see who actually made a spirit.

q: A Tequila label says nothing about being one hundred percent agave. Where may the rest of its fermentable sugar come from?
opts: Up to forty-nine percent from other agave species
Up to fifteen percent from grape must
Up to forty-nine percent from other sugars, usually cane
Up to twenty-five percent from other sugars, usually cane
exp: That style is known as mixto, though the word never appears on a label and the absence of the hundred percent claim is the only signal. The other sugar is fermented alongside the agave rather than blended in afterwards.

q: A great wheel of volcanic stone is dragged around a circular pit to crush cooked agave in the traditional way. What is that wheel called?
exp: The stone crushes rather than shreds, so fibre and juice ferment together and the spirit comes out rounder and more vegetal. A roller mill does the same job in an hour instead of a day, which is why the old method survives only where a producer chooses to pay for it.

q: A small wild agave that grows in shade beneath oaks, yields very little sugar and cannot be farmed in rows makes some of the most expensive mezcal. Name it.
exp: It grows from seed rather than from the pups that propagate espadin, so every plant harvested is one fewer in the wild. A dozen years or more in the ground yields a fraction of the sugar of a cultivated agave, and the price follows.

q: Mezcal's rules recognise a ladder of production classes, and the strictest bars mechanical shredding altogether and demands a clay pot still. Name that class.
exp: Mezcal artesanal sits a step below and allows a copper pot still and mechanical shredding, while plain Mezcal permits column stills, autoclaves and diffusers. The word describes method rather than quality, though in practice the two tend to travel together.

q: Sonora makes an agave spirit with a Mexican denomination of its own, so it may not be sold as mezcal however it is made. Name it.
exp: It is distilled from Agave angustifolia, the same species as espadin, and was outlawed in Mexico for most of the twentieth century. Raicilla in Jalisco and sotol in Chihuahua sit outside the mezcal denomination too, and sotol is not made from agave at all.

q: Botanicals are steeped in neutral spirit and the result is bottled without going near a still again. Which category does that gin fall into?
exp: Compound gin is perfectly legal and is what bathtub gin always was, but it may not call itself distilled gin. Distilled gin has to be redistilled in the presence of its botanicals, and London Dry adds that nothing beyond water and a trace of sugar may go in afterwards.
